objective: By the end of this lesson you can decide if you, the airplane, and the day are ready for safe flight: assess yourself, confirm the airplane is airworthy, do a full checklist preflight inspection, and keep checking the environment.
why: About 85 percent of accidents are blamed on "failure of the pilot to..." [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]. A careful preflight assessment is where you catch problems while you are still safe on the ground.

prereading.what: Airworthiness checks, required documents, and the visual preflight inspection (cabin, wings, fuel, oil, gear, engine).
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-12

prereading.what: IMSAFE and the PAVE checklist, including external pressures.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-8 to 2-10

prereading.what: Required inspections and flying with inoperative equipment (91.213(d)).
prereading.label: PHAK 9-8 to 9-10

prereading.what: How to build and stick to personal minimums.
prereading.label: RMH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-5

prereading.what: The PIC decides if the aircraft is in condition for safe flight.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.7

warmup: You are 20 minutes late for a flight with a friend. During preflight you see a small drip of oil under the cowling. Do you go? Who decides?

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation (14 CFR 3.5(a), as quoted in the AFH).
The approved design of the aircraft. Changes and parts must match it, e.g., life-limited parts per the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS).
A legally enforceable FAA rule issued when an unsafe condition exists in a product (aircraft, engine, propeller, appliance) and is likely to exist or develop in others of the same type design.
Installed equipment that does not work. Under 91.213(d) some items may be deferred if placarded and found not to be a hazard.
A special airworthiness certificate that lets an aircraft not meeting airworthiness rules, but safe for a specific flight, fly to where it can be fixed.
Your own limits, stricter than the rules, based on your experience and proficiency.
Self-check: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
Risk categories: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures.
Number on a sectional giving the highest terrain or obstacle elevation in a quadrant, rounded up, in hundreds of feet.

body.p: A preflight assessment checks four things before you fly: the rules, you (are you ready to be PIC), the airplane, and the environment, plus any outside pressures [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Hasty ground work eats your safety margin [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].
"Airworthy" has two parts: the aircraft conforms to its type design AND is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Paperwork proves the first part. Your eyes and hands check the second.

callout.text: No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy. The PIC is responsible for determining whether it is in condition for safe flight, and must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]. The PIC is the final authority on the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

body.p: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including AD compliance [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. But you, the PIC, still make the go decision [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

bullets: Paper check: inspections, ADs, documents, inoperative equipment.
Visual check: walk around with the AFM/POH checklist.
Self check: IMSAFE and personal minimums.
Environment check: weather, terrain, route, obstructions, airspace.

check.q: What two conditions make an aircraft airworthy?
check.a: It conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

chunks.title: Self-assessment: am I fit to fly?

body.p: You are one of the risk factors in every flight. Ask: "Am I ready for this trip?" in experience, recency, currency, physical and emotional condition [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. Being legal is not the same as being smart or safe [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

head: IMSAFE
Ask yourself
rows: Am I taking anything that could affect judgment or make me drowsy?
Pressure from work, money, health, or family? Stress hurts concentration and performance.
Drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours? One ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer, or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills.
Am I tired? Fatigue may not show until serious errors are made.

body.p: Table from [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

callout.text: No crewmember within 8 hours after any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence, while using a drug that affects faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. If you hold a medical certificate, you may not act as PIC while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition, or are taking medication or treatment for one, that would make you unable to meet that certificate's requirements [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

body.p: Personal minimums are limits stricter than the rules, based on your own experience [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]. Set them on the ground, when there is no pressure to make a trip [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

head: Weather category
Ceiling
Visibility
rows: and/or 1 mile to less than 3 miles

body.p: Categories from [[30:13|RMH Figure 2-1]]. Start your personal minimums here, then add wind and runway limits [[30:15|RMH 2-3]], [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].

callout.text: Example: the AFM lists a 15-knot maximum demonstrated crosswind, but you have only flown 10 knots. Your limit is 10 knots until a CFI trains you for more [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

check.q: You had a beer 7 hours ago and feel fine. Can you act as PIC?
check.a: No. No crewmember duties within 8 hours after any alcoholic beverage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]].

chunks.title: Is the airplane legal? Documents and inspections

body.p: Logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane. Check the logbooks or a summary of the airworthy status before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. A sample airworthiness checklist helps [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

head: Item
Requirement
Rule
rows: If carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides: an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service. May be exceeded by not more than 10 hours to reach a place to do it; the extra time counts toward the next 100
Tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months
Altimeter, static system and altitude encoder
Within the preceding 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
Inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection
Replace or recharge after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired
Within 30 days, when using VOR for IFR
Status and compliance recorded; operating with an unmet AD is a violation

callout.text: 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year. Annual done March 15 = good through March 31 next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

body.p: Documents that must be, as appropriate, on board, attached, or affixed [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]:

bullets: Airworthiness certificate, displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so passengers or crew can read it [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]], [[60:486|91.203(b)]].
Registration certificate [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]].
Radio station license, only for flights outside the U.S. or airplanes over 12,500 pounds (FCC rule) [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
Operating limitations: AFM/POH, placards, instrument markings, or a combination [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]].
Current weight and balance data, a compass correction card if required, and the external data plate (14 CFR 45.11) [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

body.p: "Appropriate" also matters: Is this the right airplane? Is it equipped for the flight (instruments, lights, radios)? Can it use the runways, carry the load, reach the altitudes, and carry enough fuel with reserves [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]], [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]? You must also know runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data for any flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

check.q: Your rental airplane is used for flight instruction for hire by the school that provides it. Which inspection does it need beyond the annual?
check.a: A 100-hour inspection (an annual may be substituted) [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

body.p: When you find inoperative equipment before flight, you have three choices: cancel, get maintenance before flight, or defer the item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Most small piston airplanes without an MEL use 91.213(d) [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
Under 91.213(d), you may take off with an item inoperative only if it is NOT [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment.
Shown as required on the aircraft's equipment list or Kinds of Operations Equipment List for this kind of flight.
Required by 91.205 or another rule for this kind of flight.
Required to work by an airworthiness directive.

body.p: Then the item must be removed (control placarded, maintenance recorded) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative," and an appropriately rated certificated pilot, or a person certificated and rated to maintain the aircraft, must decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]. If deactivation or removal involves maintenance (removal always does), certificated maintenance personnel must do it and record it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]], [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

callout.text: Example: position lights fail before a DAY flight. Follow 91.213(d): deactivate (e.g., pull the circuit breaker) and placard the switch INOPERATIVE [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. For a night flight, approved position lights are required [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]], so you cannot go.

body.p: For day VFR, 91.205(b) requires items such as airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, tachometer, oil pressure gauge, oil temperature gauge (air-cooled engine), and fuel gauges [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. If the item can't be deferred and parts aren't available, a special flight permit may let you fly it to a repair shop [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

check.q: Before a day VFR flight, the fuel gauge for one tank is dead. Can you defer it under 91.213(d)?
check.a: No. A fuel gauge for each tank is required by 91.205(b) for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(9)]], and items required by 91.205 cannot be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

chunks.title: Do it step by step: the walk-around

head: ACS skill
Standard
rows: Inspect the airplane with reference to an appropriate checklist.
Verify the airplane is in condition for safe flight and conforms to its type design.
Continue to assess the environment for safe flight.

body.p: This Task has no numeric tolerances. Use the AFM/POH checklist, or a third-party checklist based on it; each manufacturer sets its own order [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. A typical flow from the AFH:

bullets: 1. Review the logbooks or airworthy-status summary. Fix any discrepancy before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]], [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
2. As you walk up: general look, landing gear alignment, wing/fuselage/tail distortion, skin damage, fuel or oil stains and puddles [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
3. Confirm the required documents are on board [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
4. Door and cabin: door fit and latches, carpet, seat belts and harnesses, seats locked in rails, windshield clean and free of cracks [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

5. Cockpit (per AFM/POH): gear DOWN if retractable, master/alternator/magnetos OFF, control locks REMOVED, fuel selector works in all positions, trim set for takeoff, circuit breakers IN; master ON to compare fuel gauges with a visual tank check and test lights; airspeed zero, compass full of fluid, VSI zero; then master OFF [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].
6. Walk around, often counterclockwise from the cabin entry: spar lines, attach points, rivets, leading edges [[24:43|AFH 2-6]], [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
7. Fuel: quantity checked by eye, grade, sump every drain, vents clear, caps secure [[24:46|AFH 2-9]], [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
8. Oil: level and color, cap secure [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
9. Landing gear, tires, brakes [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].
10. Engine and propeller: cowling fasteners, spinner, prop blades, inside the cowling, air filter [[24:48|AFH 2-11]], [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].

head: Area
Look for (defects)
Why
rows: Distortion, ripples, bubbles, dents, creases, waves
Load stress concentrates here; deformity may mean internal damage [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]
Rivet is working loose in its hole [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]
Cracks from screw holes; cracks past a stop-drill
Dents from rocks, ice, birds, hangar rash
Some dents make the structure unairworthy [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]
Bubbles, hairline cracks, change in tap sound
Cuts, bulges, sidewall cracks, visible cords, odd wear
Any of these make the tire unairworthy [[24:48|AFH 2-11]]
Leaks, rust, worn pads, low strut
Blade damage can lead to failure [[24:49|AFH 2-12]], [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Oil leaks, fuel dye, bird nests, rags, tools, white exhaust stains

check.q: You see a black ring around several rivet heads on a wing spar line. What does it mean and what do you do?
check.a: A black-oxide film forms when a rivet works loose in its hole [[24:43|AFH 2-6]]. Do not fly; have a mechanic look at it [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

chunks.title: Fuel and oil: checks that keep the engine running

body.p: Without the right fuel quantity, grade, and quality, the engine will likely quit [[24:46|AFH 2-9]]. Always confirm the gauges by looking in each tank; ramp slope and strut height change how full the tank looks [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

bullets: Grade: 80/87 is red, 100LL is blue, 100/130 is green [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]. Never use a lower grade than required; it can cause detonation [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Jet fuel: clear or straw colored, kerosene smell, oily feel. A piston engine on jet fuel may run long enough to take off, then fail [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].
Water: beads or bubbles at the bottom of the sample jar. Keep sampling until no water or dirt shows [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Sediment: dirt, or small dark specks from rubber seals [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].
Sump every tank drain and the strainer during preflight and after refueling, in the order the AFM/POH says [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Vents: a blocked vent can cause fuel starvation. A rush of air when you crack the cap may mean a vent problem [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Stains: fuel stains anywhere near a tank mean probable leakage, no matter how old [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

body.p: Oil lubricates, carries heat, and holds dirt. Check it each preflight and at each refueling [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. A cold engine reads higher on the dipstick than a warm one. Oil that darkens fast just after an oil change may point to cylinder problems [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

callout.text: Don't leave fuel and oil to line service alone. Watch the fueling, check the grade and amount, and make sure every cap is secure [[24:47|AFH 2-10]], [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

check.q: Your first fuel sample has clear beads at the bottom of the cup. What next?
check.a: That is water. Keep sampling until no water or contamination appears; significant or repeated water needs maintenance [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

callout.text: Before every flight, the PIC must become familiar with all available information about it. For a flight under IFR or not in the vicinity of an airport, that includes weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight can't be completed, and known ATC delays. For any flight: runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

head: Factor
What to check
rows: Ceiling and visibility (higher in mountains); weather may differ from forecast, so have alternatives; winds and crosswind; strong winds aloft in mountains; thunderstorms; icing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Pick safe altitudes in advance from VFR and IFR charts; use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Lighting; NOTAMs for closed runways and lights out; shorter or obstructed fields [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Choose it wisely: if the engine quits, nearby airports matter most [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Survival gear over remote areas; check airspace and TFRs along the route [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]
Check all lights; carry at least two flashlights [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]

body.p: The MEF is the highest elevation in a quadrant, terrain or obstacles like towers, rounded up to the next 100 feet [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]]. Example: a tower top at 2,649 ft MSL + 100 ft possible error = 2,749, raised to 2,800. The chart shows "28" [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]].

Keep assessing after takeoff. Weather can change drastically over time and distance [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]]. The 3P model (Perceive, Process, Perform) is a continuous loop [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]]. Situational awareness starts in preflight and ends only when the airplane is tied down or hangared [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

check.q: A sectional quadrant shows "28" with a small 8. What does it mean?
check.a: MEF of 2,800 ft MSL: the highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrant, rounded up [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]].

body.p: PAVE helps you see hazards: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. Then process each one with CARE (Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors) and act with TEAM (Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate) [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]], [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]].

bullets: Pilot: a pilot with 4 hours of sleep, asked to fly 750 miles in marginal weather, said no. The boss later agreed [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Aircraft: a pilot saw a small oil drip, delayed, and a mechanic found a loose oil cooler hose fitting [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Environment: a pilot assumed wake turbulence from a heavy jet would not matter and made a hard landing [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

callout.text: If you hear yourself say a discrepancy is "probably" okay, that is the time for a reality check [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]], [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

body.p: Raise your minimums when conditions add risk. The RMH suggests adjustments such as adding at least 500 ft to ceiling, 1/2 mile to visibility, 500 ft to runway length, or subtracting at least 5 knots from winds, for factors like fatigue, an unfamiliar airplane, an unfamiliar airport, or deadlines. Adjust for each factor [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]]. Example: night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday = +1,000 ft ceiling, +1 mile visibility, +1,000 ft runway [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

bullets: Don't change your minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Change one variable at a time [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Talk to a CFI before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: Ways to lower risk for a marginal-weather trip: wait, take an instrument-rated pilot, delay, cancel, or drive [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

check.q: Your personal minimum is a 3,000 ft ceiling. The weather is 2,800 ft, and your friends are waiting. Should you lower your minimum today?
check.a: No. Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight; adjust only when there is time and no pressure [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: External pressures push you to finish a flight, often at the cost of safety: someone waiting, a passenger you don't want to let down, wanting to impress, "get-there-itis," or pride [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]], [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]]. Managing them is the single most important key to risk management, because they can make you ignore every other risk [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

bullets: Allow time for an extra fuel stop or a weather landing [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Have backup plans (even airline reservations) for must-be-there trips [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Tell people waiting that you may be late, and manage passengers' expectations [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Carry a small overnight kit so you don't feel you must get home [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

callout.text: Be ready for and accept delays. The goal is to manage risk, not create hazards [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

body.p: Security is part of the preflight too:

bullets: Escort passengers on the ramp if they aren't under your direct supervision, for safety and ramp security. Supervise baggage loading [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
Secure the airplane after flight: control locks and anti-theft security locks; consider prop security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
Don't enter a Security Identification Display Area (SIDA) without authorization and ID; brief passengers [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]], [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Report suspicious activity to the TSA through AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287 [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
You must show your airman and medical certificates to the TSA on request (49 CFR 1540) [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Check NOTAMs and TFRs during planning; pilots who don't follow national security rules may be intercepted, detained, and interviewed [[34:12|AIM 5-6-2]].

check.q: Why does the PHAK call external pressure management the most important key to risk management?
check.a: It is the one risk category that can cause a pilot to ignore all the other risk factors [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

bullets: Doing the preflight from memory. Pilots who don't take checklists seriously become complacent [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
Rushing. Hasty ground operations shrink the safety margin [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].
Trusting the fuel gauges without looking in the tanks [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].
Taking one small fuel sample. In bad cases the whole sample may be water [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Leaving fuel and oil to line service with no oversight [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Checking only the visible part of each tire. Move the airplane slightly to see the full tire [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].
Forgetting the control lock or fuel caps [[24:42|AFH 2-5]], [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].
Treating "legal" as "safe" [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].
Stopping the assessment at takeoff. Keep perceiving, processing, and performing [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

callout.text: Say each checklist item out loud and touch it. If anything looks wrong, stop and ask a mechanic [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

check.q: Why should you move the airplane a little during the tire check?
check.a: To see the whole tire. With many pilots flying it, what happened to the tires on earlier flights is unknown [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].

scenario.title: Saturday trip to see a friend
scenario.setup: You are a new private pilot. A friend is waiting at an airport 90 NM away for lunch. You slept 5 hours after a stressful week. The club airplane's landing light is placarded INOP by maintenance. Your first fuel sample shows clear beads at the bottom. Destination weather is 2,500 ft overcast, forecast to improve, and a ridge lies along the direct route. While you preflight, a stranger without a badge wanders across the ramp toward the parked airplanes.

questions.q: Pilot: how does your night of sleep and stressful week affect the go decision?
questions.a: Run IMSAFE: Stress and Fatigue are both flagged; fatigue may not show until serious errors are made [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. RMH suggests raising your minimums for fatigue or stress (e.g., at least 500 ft more ceiling) [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]]. A short local flight or a delay may be the smart choice.

questions.q: Aircraft: is the inoperative landing light a no-go for a day flight?
questions.a: Not if 91.213(d) is met: not required for day VFR by type certification, the equipment list/KOEL, 91.205, or an AD; deactivated or removed and placarded; and found not to be a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. Check the airplane's equipment list in the POH.

questions.q: Aircraft: what about the water in the fuel?
questions.a: Keep sampling until no water or contamination appears. Significant or repeated water means maintenance should look at it [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

questions.q: Environment: how do you handle the ceiling and the ridge?
questions.a: Compare 2,500 ft to your personal minimums, plan a safe altitude from the chart and MEFs, and pick a route that keeps airports nearby [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. Weather may differ from the forecast, so have an alternative and be willing to divert [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

questions.q: External pressures: your friend is waiting. How do you remove that pressure?
questions.a: Call and say you may be late or may not come. Be ready to accept delays [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

questions.q: Security: what do you do about the stranger?
questions.a: Report suspicious activity to the TSA through AOPA's Airport Watch Program (866-427-3287) or to airport security [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. When you leave, lock the airplane and install control and security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

skills.do: Do a full preflight inspection of the airplane while following the AFM/POH checklist (or one based on it), item by item, not from memory.
skills.practice: Do every preflight with the checklist in hand, out loud. Ask your CFI to watch one preflight a week and point out anything skipped [[24:36|AFH 1-15]], [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

skills.do: Show the examiner the inspection status (annual, ELT, transponder, ADs), the required documents, and that the airplane is in condition for safe flight. Explain what you'd do with a discrepancy or inoperative item.
skills.practice: Build your own airworthiness checklist like AFH Figure 2-4 for your training airplane and fill it in from the logbooks [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. Practice a 91.213(d) decision on a pretend inoperative item [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner how you assessed yourself (IMSAFE, personal minimums) and that you are fit for this flight.
skills.practice: Write your personal minimums using the RMH worksheets, and run IMSAFE before every lesson [[30:13|RMH 2-1]], [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

skills.do: Keep checking weather, terrain, route, obstructions, and airspace before and during the flight, and say what would make you change the plan.
skills.practice: On each lesson, brief one environmental hazard before flight and name your divert option. Use the 3P loop in flight [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, quoting 14 CFR 3.5(a), an aircraft is "airworthy" when it:
options: Has a current annual inspection
Conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation
Has an airworthiness certificate on board
Has no inoperative equipment
quiz.why: Airworthy means the aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

quiz.q: The last annual inspection was signed off on March 15, 2026. Through what date may the airplane be flown without a new annual?
options: March 14, 2027
March 15, 2027
March 31, 2027
April 30, 2027
quiz.why: 12 calendar months runs to the last day of the same month the following year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

quiz.q: To use the ATC transponder, it must have been tested and inspected within the preceding:
options: 12 calendar months
24 calendar months
100 hours
30 days
quiz.why: Within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

quiz.q: Before a day VFR flight in a small piston airplane with no MEL, you find a position light out. Which is correct under 91.213(d)?
options: You may never fly with any inoperative equipment
Deactivate it, placard it INOPERATIVE, and determine it is not a hazard
Write it on the squawk sheet and fly; no placard needed
You need a special flight permit
quiz.why: Provided the light is not required by the type certification, the equipment list/KOEL, 91.205 or an AD for this flight, it must be removed or deactivated and placarded, and a pilot or mechanic must determine it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

quiz.q: Your first fuel sample shows bead-like droplets at the bottom of the jar. You should:
options: Fly; a few drops are normal
Keep sampling until no water or contamination appears
Add fuel to dilute it
Run the engine at high power to clear it
quiz.why: Water shows as beads at the bottom; continue sampling until none appears [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

quiz.q: Which is true about alcohol and acting as a crewmember?
options: Wait 4 hours after drinking
Wait 8 hours, and alcohol concentration must be below 0.04
Wait 12 hours; no BAC limit
Wait 24 hours
quiz.why: No crewmember duties within 8 hours after drinking or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].

quiz.q: On a sectional, the Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) shows:
options: The lowest safe altitude for IFR
The highest terrain or obstacle elevation in the quadrant, rounded up to the next 100 ft
The airport elevation
The floor of Class E airspace
quiz.why: MEF is the highest elevation in a quadrant, including terrain and obstacles, rounded up to the nearest 100 ft [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]].

quiz.q: Which PAVE category does the PHAK call the single most important key to risk management?
options: Pilot
Aircraft
Environment
External pressures
quiz.why: External pressures can cause a pilot to ignore all other risk factors [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

takeaways: Airworthy = conforms to type design + in condition for safe operation; the PIC decides [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
Check paperwork first: annual (12 calendar months), 100-hour if for hire, transponder (24 months), ELT, ADs, documents.
Inoperative equipment: cancel, fix, or defer under 91.213(d) with placard and a no-hazard decision.
Use the checklist every time; look in the tanks and sump every drain.
Run IMSAFE and stick to personal minimums set on the ground.
External pressures are the biggest risk; be ready to accept delays.
cfi_notes: Have students fill in an airworthiness checklist like AFH Figure 2-4 from the real logbooks of the training airplane; examiners often ask to see inspection and AD status.
Set up 'what if' items during preflight (a pretend inop light, a dark fuel sample) and make the student talk through 91.213(d) or the sumping procedure.
Watch for students reading the checklist but not looking at the item. Ask them to touch and say each item.
Calendar-month math trips students up. Practice with a few dates (annual, ELT, transponder).
Use the PHAK Gayle example (Figures 2-11 and 2-12) to show PAVE + CARE + TEAM on a real trip [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]], [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].
Examiners often probe external pressures and self-assessment with a scenario. Have students say out loud when they'd cancel.
Security is easy to forget: ask where the control lock, prop lock and tie-downs go, and how to report suspicious activity.
gaps: Airplane-specific preflight items (inspection order, number and location of fuel drains, oil capacity and limits, equipment list/KOEL, fuel grade) must come from the training airplane's POH/AFM; the lesson uses the AFH's generic guidance.
14 CFR Part 3 (3.5(a) definition of airworthy) is not in the resource set; the definition is cited through AFH 2-1.

Aviation security: sources give only AIM 2-3-15 (SIDA, Airport Watch, 49 CFR 1540), AIM 5-6 (national security/TFRs), and AFH securing/escort guidance. No TSA general aviation security guidelines are in the resources; 49 CFR 1540 itself is not included.
The ACS Skills elements for this Task give no numeric tolerances; the skills table lists the element text only.

activities.title: Spot the IMSAFE warning sign
activities.intro: Tap an IMSAFE item, then the warning sign that goes with it.

pairs.r: Your stuffy nose might be the start of a cold
You took an allergy pill that can make you drowsy
Money and family problems are hurting your concentration
You had a glass of wine 6 hours ago
You slept only 4 hours last night
You are very upset after hearing some sad news

activities.title: Defer it or fix it?
activities.intro: Tap a broken item, then tap what you can do with it. Assume a small airplane with no MEL.
buckets: May defer: deactivate, placard, no-hazard call

items.t: Position lights, before a day flight
Landing light on a day flight, not required by any list, rule, or AD
Position lights, before a night flight
Airspeed indicator, before a day flight
Magnetic compass, before a day flight
An item an airworthiness directive says must work
An item the equipment list shows as required for this flight

activities.title: Start the preflight in the right order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in the order the AFH describes, then tap Check.
steps: Review the logbooks or the airworthy-status summary
Look over the whole airplane as you walk up to it
Check that the cabin door fits and latches smoothly
Master, alternator, and magnetos OFF; control lock removed
Master ON: note the fuel gauges, check the lights
Master OFF, then walk around the outside of the airplane

activities.title: True or false: fuel, risk, and security

cards.s: If the fuel gauges read full, you can skip looking in the tanks.
cards.why: No. Always confirm the gauges by looking at the fuel level in each tank. Ramp slope and strut height can change how full a tank is [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

cards.s: A fuel stain near a tank is a sign of probable leakage, even if it looks old.
cards.why: Yes. Fuel stains anywhere near a tank need a closer look, no matter how old they appear [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

cards.s: Weather can change a lot over time and distance, so you keep checking the environment after takeoff.
cards.why: Yes. Weather can change drastically over time and distance [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]], and the 3P decision loop keeps running in flight [[1:56|PHAK 2-17]].

cards.s: To lower your personal minimums, change ceiling, visibility, and wind all at the same time.
cards.why: No. Change one variable at a time, and talk to a CFI before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

cards.s: Passengers who are not under your direct supervision should have an escort on the ramp.
cards.why: Yes. An escort keeps them safe and keeps the ramp secure. You should also supervise baggage loading [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

cards.s: Holding a pilot certificate lets you walk into a Security Identification Display Area (SIDA).
cards.why: No. Entering a SIDA is prohibited without authorization and proper identification displayed [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].

final_quiz.q: The logbooks for your club airplane show every inspection and AD up to date. On the walk-around you find a cracked propeller spinner with a missing fastener. Is the airplane airworthy?
options: Yes. Current paperwork means it is airworthy.
Yes, if you write it on the squawk sheet after the flight.
No. It must also be in condition for safe operation, and this spinner is not.
Yes, because only the owner decides if it is airworthy.
final_quiz.why: Airworthy means the aircraft conforms to its type design AND is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. Cracks or missing fasteners make a spinner unairworthy [[24:49|AFH 2-12]], and the PIC decides if the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You took a cold medicine whose label warns it may cause drowsiness. You feel fine and had no alcohol. What does 14 CFR 91.17 say?
options: You may not act as a crewmember while using a drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety.
You may fly once 8 hours have passed since the last dose.
The rule covers only prescription drugs, so you may fly.
You may fly if another pilot rides along.
final_quiz.why: No crewmember duties while using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]. The 8-hour rule is for alcohol. IMSAFE asks if a medicine might affect your judgment or make you drowsy [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane must carry an ELT. The ELT was last inspected on September 9, 2025. Today is September 25, 2026. May you fly?
options: No. The inspection ran out on September 9, 2026.
Yes. It is good through September 30, 2026.
No. ELTs must be inspected every 6 months.
Yes. ELTs need an inspection only every 24 calendar months.
final_quiz.why: The ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Twelve calendar months run to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], so September 30, 2026.

final_quiz.q: A school airplane used for paid flight lessons had its last 100-hour inspection at 2,100.0 hours time in service. It reached 2,200.0 hours away from base and flew 6 more hours to reach a shop, arriving at 2,206.0, where it was inspected. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
options: 2,300.0 hours
2,306.0 hours
2,310.0 hours
2,316.0 hours
final_quiz.why: You may go over the 100 hours by up to 10 hours to reach a place where the inspection can be done, but the extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. So the next one is due 100 hours after 2,200.0: at 2,300.0.

final_quiz.q: Before a day VFR flight in a small airplane with no MEL, you find the tachometer does not work. No parts or mechanics are available at this airport. What can you do?
options: Deactivate it, placard it INOPERATIVE, and fly your trip
Fly your trip and set power by the sound of the engine
Fly your trip if your CFI decides it is not a hazard
Get a special flight permit to fly the airplane to a repair shop
final_quiz.why: A tachometer is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(4)]], so it cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. If maintenance or parts are not available, a special flight permit can let you fly it to a place where it can be fixed [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: The picture shows cracks at wingtip screw holes, each ending in a small drilled hole. On your preflight, one crack has grown past its drilled hole. What should you do?
options: Fly. A stop-drilled crack is already repaired.
Don't fly. Have a mechanic look at it, since it may lead to in-flight failure.
Fly, but keep your airspeed low.
Cover it with tape and report it after the flight.
final_quiz.why: Stop-drilling is done to keep a crack from growing. A crack that has continued past the stop-drilled hole may lead to in-flight failure [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]. Talk to a properly rated mechanic about anything out of place [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: During the cockpit check, one flight instrument does not read zero on the ground. Which one may you, the pilot, adjust yourself?
options: Mechanical vertical speed indicator (VSI)
Airspeed indicator
Turn coordinator
Magnetic compass
final_quiz.why: The mechanical VSI is the only flight instrument a pilot may adjust; a small screwdriver can zero it. All others must be adjusted by an FAA-certificated repairman or mechanic [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane needs 100LL or a higher grade of fuel. The fuel sample from one tank is red. What does that tell you?
options: It is 100LL, so you can fly.
It is jet fuel, which is fine for takeoff.
It is 80/87, a lower grade. Don't fly; it can cause detonation.
It is 100/130, a higher grade, so you can fly.
final_quiz.why: 80/87 is dyed red, 100LL is blue, and 100/130 is green [[24:44|AFH 2-7]]. Never use a lower grade than required: detonation can badly damage the engine in a very short time [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: During preflight you crack open a fuel cap and hear a rush of air. What could it mean?
options: Nothing. This is normal on every airplane.
The tank was overfilled.
There is water in the tank.
There could be a problem with the fuel vent system, which can lead to fuel starvation.
final_quiz.why: A rush of air when you crack the cap may mean a serious vent problem. If air can't enter the tank as fuel is used, the result is fuel starvation and engine failure [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: In one sectional quadrant, the highest thing is a tower with its top at 3,412 ft MSL, more than 200 ft above the highest terrain in the quadrant. What MEF will the chart show?
final_quiz.why: For a man-made obstacle, add 100 ft for possible error (3,412 + 100 = 3,512), then round up to the next 100 ft: 3,600. The last two digits are not shown, so the chart shows "36" [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a short local flight in the traffic pattern at your home airport. What preflight information does 14 CFR 91.103 require for every flight, including this one?
options: Alternatives if the planned flight can't be completed
Known traffic delays that ATC has told you about
Runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data
Fuel requirements for an alternate airport
final_quiz.why: Runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance data are required for any flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. Alternatives, fuel requirements, and known delays are listed for IFR flights or flights not in the vicinity of an airport [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your baseline night personal minimums are a 5,000 ft ceiling and 8 miles visibility. Tonight you plan a cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday. Following the RMH example, what minimums fit tonight?
options: 4,000 ft and 7 miles
5,000 ft and 8 miles, no change
6,000 ft and 8 miles
6,000 ft and 9 miles
final_quiz.why: For a night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday, the RMH suggests adding 1,000 ft to the ceiling, 1 mile to visibility, and 1,000 ft to runway length [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. 5,000 + 1,000 = 6,000 ft and 8 + 1 = 9 miles.

final_quiz.q: You will fly home Sunday evening because you must be at work Monday morning. Which step best removes the pressure to fly home in bad weather?
options: Promise your boss you will be at work by 8 AM
Carry a small overnight kit and have a backup plan, such as an airline ticket
Lower your personal minimums for the trip home
Skip the weather briefing so you can leave sooner
final_quiz.why: Carrying an overnight kit and making backup plans, even airline reservations, for must-be-there trips releases external pressure [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]]. Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: At the airport, a TSA official asks to see your pilot certificate. What should you do?
options: Show it. Federal rules require you to present it to TSA on request.
Decline. Only the FAA may ask to see it.
Show it only if you are flying for hire.
Show your logbook instead.
final_quiz.why: 49 CFR 1540 requires anyone holding an FAA airman certificate, medical certificate, authorization, or license to present it for inspection when TSA asks [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
